books.optimization: The Art of Finding the Best · Book 7

algebra/variables.title: An equation turns a bill into a question
algebra/variables.story: A book costs ₹120 and each notebook costs ₹35. Your bill is ₹330. Instead of guessing notebook counts, give the unknown a name: n. The equation records the story; solving it finds a value that makes the story true.
algebra/variables.predict: Would six notebooks fit the bill? What must stay equal when you subtract the book price?
rows: Divide by the price per notebook
algebra/variables.relationship: The equals sign asserts that two expressions have the same value. n is an unknown count; 35 is a rate in rupees per notebook. More complex stories can use several variables or squared terms without changing what equality means.
algebra/variables.ml: A model also expresses a relationship: price = baseline + rate × quantity. In model fitting, observed quantities are supplied and parameters are estimated.
algebra/variables.caution: This book example and the delivery-price playground use different prices. Read the rule shown by each activity before calculating.
algebra/variables.alt: A balanced scale represents a ₹120 book and six ₹35 notebooks equalling ₹330.

algebra/functions.title: One permitted input, one defined output
algebra/functions.story: A vending machine accepts a selection and follows a rule. A mathematical function does the same: each permitted input has exactly one output. Different inputs may share an output.
algebra/functions.predict: For f(x) = 2x + 1, what comes out when x is 3? Would one input producing two different outputs still define a function?
algebra/functions.relationship: Writing f(x) names the result of applying f to x; it does not mean f multiplied by x. The domain tells us which inputs the rule permits. 1/(x−2) excludes 2; a 40-seat bus also imposes whole-number passenger counts from 0 to 40.
algebra/functions.ml: Features enter a prediction function and a predicted value comes out. Check both the formal input constraints and whether the situation resembles the data used to develop the model.
algebra/functions.caution: A mathematically valid input is not automatically a reliable prediction. Training coverage and the formal domain are different ideas.
algebra/functions.alt: Inputs 1, 3 and 5 pass through f(x) = 2x + 1 to outputs 3, 7 and 11.

algebra/graphs.title: See where two pricing stories cross
algebra/graphs.story: QuickRide charges ₹50 plus ₹10 per kilometre. Steady charges ₹110 plus ₹7 per kilometre. A graph puts both rules on the same axes so you can see when the cheaper choice changes.
algebra/graphs.predict: Which service is cheaper at 10 km? Could the answer reverse on a longer journey?
algebra/graphs.relationship: The intercept is the starting charge. The slope is the added cost per kilometre. Setting 50 + 10d = 110 + 7d gives d = 20: the crossing represents equal prices, not equal slopes.
algebra/graphs.ml: A prediction line makes starting level and sensitivity visible. Scatter plots show pairs of observed measurements; a fitted curve is a model, not the observations themselves.
algebra/graphs.caution: A line shows a constant rate. Curves, histograms and bar charts answer different questions; do not force every relationship into a line.
algebra/graphs.alt: QuickRide starts lower but rises faster; the two lines cross at 20 km and ₹250.

algebra/powers.title: Repeated growth leads to the number e
algebra/powers.story: Adding a fixed amount and multiplying by a fixed factor create very different futures. Now divide a 100% annual growth rate into smaller and smaller compounding intervals. The total approaches a finite limit rather than increasing without bound.
algebra/powers.predict: Starting with 1, which grows faster after six steps: adding 5 each time or doubling? Does compounding 100% more frequently make the final factor infinite?
algebra/powers.relationship: e is the limiting factor (1 + 1/n)^n as n grows. More generally, e^x is the exponential whose local rate of change equals its current value. That property makes it especially useful for describing continuous proportional change.
algebra/powers.ml: Natural exponentials appear in sigmoid probabilities and softmax. Their derivatives have a simple form, helping us trace how changing a parameter changes a loss.
algebra/powers.caution: A growth rate of 100% is an illustrative assumption. e is a mathematical constant, not an investment promise. The paper-folding example is an idealized thickness calculation.
algebra/powers.alt: More frequent compounding approaches e ≈ 2.71828; annual and monthly values lie below the limit.

algebra/logarithms.title: Ask how many multiplications happened
algebra/logarithms.story: If a quantity doubles repeatedly, how many doublings reach a million? Exponentials tell you the result of growth; logarithms recover the exponent. About 19.93 doublings reach exactly a million, while 20 whole doublings first exceed it.
algebra/logarithms.predict: If 2³ = 8, what question does log₂(8) answer? Why should a confidently wrong probability have a large negative-log penalty?
headers: Probability of the observed class p
algebra/logarithms.relationship: log_b(a) is the exponent needed to turn b into a. ln uses base e. For positive a and c, ln(ac) = ln(a) + ln(c), converting products into sums.
algebra/logarithms.ml: Log-likelihoods turn many tiny probability products into manageable sums. Negative log-loss penalizes assigning very little probability to what actually happened.
algebra/logarithms.caution: Real logarithms require positive arguments and a base greater than zero other than 1. The finite table excludes p = 0, where −ln(p) has no finite value.
algebra/logarithms.alt: The negative-log curve rises sharply as the probability assigned to the true class approaches zero.

linear/vectors.title: A vector keeps measurements together
linear/vectors.story: Walking three steps east and four north gives one displacement: (3, 4). The pair preserves both components, while its length summarizes how far you are from the starting point.
linear/vectors.predict: If you double both components, what happens to direction and length?
linear/vectors.relationship: Order matters: (3, 4) and (4, 3) represent different measurements. Vector operations act on matching components. Geometry helps you see the operations; feature names tell you what they mean.
linear/vectors.ml: A house can be represented by area, room count and age. Keep a consistent order and sensible scaling when comparing houses.
linear/vectors.caution: A feature vector mixes measurements with different units. Its raw Euclidean length is not automatically a meaningful similarity measure.
linear/vectors.alt: Adding arrows combines displacements; the vector (3, 4) has horizontal component 3, vertical component 4 and length 5.

linear/dot.title: A weighted sum becomes a compatibility score
linear/dot.story: Anaya rates two tastes (5, 1). Bilal rates them (4, 2), and Chitra (1, 5). Multiply matching ratings and add: this is a dot product.
linear/dot.predict: Who has a larger dot product with Anaya? Could simply using bigger numbers change a score without changing direction?
linear/dot.relationship: a · b adds component-wise products. Its magnitude reflects both lengths and alignment. Dividing by both nonzero lengths produces cosine similarity, which isolates directional alignment.
linear/dot.ml: Linear predictions are weighted sums of features. Dot products also appear in similarity search and attention scores, with context-specific scaling and interpretation.
linear/dot.caution: Cosine is undefined for a zero vector. Orthogonal vectors are geometrically perpendicular; that alone does not establish statistical independence.
linear/dot.alt: Bilal’s taste vector points close to Anaya’s; Chitra’s points away. Raw dot product and normalized alignment are compared.

linear/matrix-vector.title: Make one prediction for every row
linear/matrix-vector.story: Three students have measurements (5, 2), (3, 1) and (8, 4). With weights (4, 3), the same weighted rule can score every student at once.
linear/matrix-vector.predict: Which numbers should be multiplied together for the second student?
linear/matrix-vector.relationship: A 3×2 matrix X times a two-component vector w produces three scores. Each output is one row’s dot product with the same weights. Dimensions explain why the operation fits.
linear/matrix-vector.ml: A dataset can use rows for observations and columns for features. Xw computes predictions for all rows with one consistent model.
linear/matrix-vector.caution: Rows and columns need named meanings. A compatible shape is necessary, but does not guarantee that the chosen features or model are useful.
linear/matrix-vector.alt: A three-row, two-column matrix times weights 4 and 3 produces scores 26, 15 and 44.

linear/matrix-matrix.title: Composition has a right-to-left order
linear/matrix-matrix.story: Stretching a shape and then rotating it need not produce the same result as rotating first. A matrix product packages a sequence of linear operations.
linear/matrix-matrix.predict: If B acts first and A second, should the composite be AB or BA?
linear/matrix-matrix.relationship: ABx means A(Bx): the rightmost operation acts first. In general AB ≠ BA. The inner dimensions must agree, and each output entry is a row–column dot product.
linear/matrix-matrix.ml: Batched predictions and linear transformations use matrix products. A neural layer adds a bias and usually a nonlinearity; composition is more than a chain of matrix products alone.
linear/matrix-matrix.caution: The order convention here uses column vectors. Read the representation before transferring a formula into code that stores row vectors.
linear/matrix-matrix.alt: Stretch then rotate and rotate then stretch put the same L-shaped figure in different locations.

linear/transform.title: A matrix moves a whole space
linear/transform.story: Rather than move each point separately, describe what happens to the coordinate directions. A linear transformation applies that same rule everywhere.
linear/transform.predict: Where will the point (3, 2) go if horizontal distances double but vertical distances stay fixed?
linear/transform.relationship: The columns show where the basis vectors go. Linear maps preserve vector addition and scalar multiplication; translation needs an added offset.
linear/transform.ml: Feature transformations can rotate, rescale or compress a representation before prediction. Scaling also changes the geometry an optimizer sees.
linear/transform.caution: A visual transformation does not itself learn a better representation. Its usefulness depends on the problem and how it was selected.
linear/transform.alt: A unit-square figure is stretched, rotated and sheared by three different matrices.

linear/span.title: Which directions can your measurements reach?
linear/span.story: Two direction vectors can cover a plane if neither is a multiple of the other. If they align, their combinations stay on one line: a dimension of information is missing.
linear/span.predict: Can two arrows pointing along the same line reconstruct every point in a plane?
linear/span.relationship: Span is the set of all linear combinations. Rank counts independent output directions, rather than merely counting rows or columns.
linear/span.ml: Redundant features can make parameter estimates ambiguous. A higher number of columns does not guarantee more independent information.
linear/span.caution: Rank deficiency can yield no solution or many solutions to a system, depending on the target. It does not always mean there is no solution.
linear/span.alt: Two intersecting equations have one common solution; parallel equations have none.

linear/inverse.title: Recover the inputs when information survives
linear/inverse.story: Two conditions, 2x + y = 11 and x + 3y = 18, describe the same pair of unknowns. Their crossing is (3, 5). An invertible transformation lets us recover that unique input.
linear/inverse.predict: Substitute (3, 5) into both conditions. Does satisfying just one equation solve the whole problem?
linear/inverse.relationship: For A = [[2,1],[1,3]], det(A)=5 and A⁻¹ = (1/5)[[3,−1],[−1,2]]. A nonzero determinant makes this square system invertible.
linear/inverse.ml: Solving systems underlies estimation and transformations. Numerical libraries usually solve a system directly rather than explicitly constructing an inverse.
linear/inverse.caution: A small determinant alone is not a scale-independent conditioning test. Rectangular least-squares problems need different tools.
linear/inverse.alt: The lines 2x + y = 11 and x + 3y = 18 intersect at (3, 5).

linear/eigen.title: Find directions a transformation does not turn
linear/eigen.story: Most arrows change direction under a transformation. Some stay on their original line: only their length or orientation changes. Those special directions are eigenvector directions.
linear/eigen.predict: For A = [[2,1],[1,2]], what happens to (1,1)? What about (1,−1)?
linear/eigen.relationship: Av = λv says a nonzero vector v remains on its own line. A negative λ reverses orientation; λ = 0 collapses that vector to zero.
linear/eigen.ml: For a centered dataset, eigenvectors of its symmetric covariance matrix identify principal directions. PCA can retain high-variance directions while discarding others.
linear/eigen.caution: The ellipse-axis picture applies to this symmetric example. An arbitrary real matrix need not have a full set of real eigenvectors. PCA preserves variance, not necessarily predictive usefulness.
linear/eigen.alt: For a symmetric matrix, diagonal eigenvector directions stretch by factors 3 and 1, turning a circle into an ellipse.

calculus/why.title: A speedometer asks about one moment
calculus/why.story: A falling ball follows d(t) = 5t² metres. Between t=1 and t=2 it covers 15 metres, but that average does not tell us its speed at exactly t=1. Shrink the interval to discover a local rate.
calculus/why.predict: As the interval after one second shrinks, will the average speed approach 15, 10 or zero?
calculus/why.relationship: The derivative is the limit of average rates as a nonzero interval shrinks, when that limit exists. For d = 5t², d′ = 10t. At one second, speed is 10 m/s.
calculus/why.ml: A derivative measures local sensitivity: how a prediction or loss responds to a small input or parameter change.
calculus/why.caution: The existing car playground uses t² rather than 5t². Its derivative is 2t. The reasoning transfers; the numerical speeds differ.
calculus/why.alt: For d = 5t², secants from t=1 approach the tangent slope 10 m/s as their intervals shrink.

calculus/secants.title: A tangent is the limit of nearby comparisons
calculus/secants.story: A secant compares two distinct points. As the second point approaches the first, its slope may approach a limiting value. A tangent represents that local direction.
calculus/secants.predict: Why can we shrink h toward zero but not substitute zero directly into a difference quotient?
calculus/secants.relationship: [f(x+h)−f(x)]/h divides output change by input change. A corner may give different limits from opposite sides, so a derivative need not exist everywhere.
calculus/secants.ml: Finite differences estimate gradients and help check implemented derivatives, but very small steps can magnify floating-point error.
calculus/secants.caution: A tangent is defined by local limiting direction. It may cross the curve elsewhere; “touches at only one point” is not a general definition.
calculus/secants.alt: A tangent follows local slope while a secant connects separated points on the curve.

calculus/rules.title: Differentiate a chain one link at a time
calculus/rules.story: For y = (3x+1)², the outer square responds to the inner value, and the inner value responds to x. Both responses matter.
calculus/rules.predict: At x=1, would 2(3x+1) alone account for the inner rule changing three times as fast?
calculus/rules.relationship: The chain rule multiplies local rates: dy/dx = (dy/du)(du/dx). Sum and constant-multiple rules let us differentiate a larger expression one piece at a time.
calculus/rules.ml: Backpropagation applies the chain rule through a computational graph. Each local operation contributes a derivative to the parameter’s final effect on loss.
calculus/rules.caution: Classical ReLU has no derivative at zero. Software uses a specified convention there; do not mistake that convention for smoothness.
calculus/rules.alt: The inner rule multiplies sensitivity by 3 and the outer square by 8; together their derivative at x=1 is 24.

calculus/practice.title: A flat slope needs a second question
calculus/practice.story: A tea stall models revenue as R(p) = 200p − 10p² for prices between 0 and 20. Revenue rises, reaches a top, then falls. A zero derivative identifies a candidate, not automatically a maximum.
calculus/practice.predict: Could zero slope mean a valley or a temporary flat point instead of a peak?
calculus/practice.relationship: R′(p) = 200 − 20p is zero at p=10. Here R″ = −20 confirms downward curvature, and checking the allowed endpoints completes the comparison.
calculus/practice.ml: Optimization asks whether a stationary point is useful and whether boundaries or other candidates matter. A zero gradient alone does not establish a good solution.
calculus/practice.caution: x³ has zero slope at zero without a local maximum or minimum. The tea rule is a simplified demand assumption, not a business forecast.
calculus/practice.alt: Revenue peaks at price 10 with value 1000; its derivative changes from positive to negative.

calculus/lab.title: A gradient gathers several sensitivities
calculus/lab.story: For f(x,y) = x² + 2y², changing x and changing y can affect the same output differently. A partial derivative isolates one coordinate while holding the other fixed.
calculus/lab.predict: At (3,2), which coordinate has the larger local sensitivity? What happens if both coordinates move against their derivatives?
calculus/lab.relationship: The gradient collects partial derivatives. A descent step subtracts a scaled gradient using the same pre-update point for every component.
calculus/lab.ml: Training repeatedly predicts, measures loss, computes a gradient and updates parameters. Step size matters: a large step can overshoot instead of improving the objective.
calculus/lab.caution: This book surface uses 2y²; the multivariable playground uses 3y². Steepest direction is local and depends on the coordinate scale and chosen geometry.
calculus/lab.alt: Gradient-descent steps cross elliptical contours toward the minimum of x² + 2y².

calculus/debug.title: Trace a prediction forward and its error backward
calculus/debug.story: A single neuron uses x=2, w=0.5 and b=0. Its score z=wx+b is 1; the sigmoid probability is about 0.731. For a true label of 1, negative log-loss is about 0.313.
calculus/debug.predict: If the model is not confident enough in the true class, should increasing this positive weight raise or lower its loss locally?
calculus/debug.relationship: The output error travels backward through each local relationship. The same original prediction supplies both gradients; do not recompute one midway through the update.
calculus/debug.ml: This scalar walkthrough connects sigmoid, log-loss and chain rule. It is a reading example; the existing debug activity deliberately uses squared error and a different rule.
calculus/debug.caution: A matching update direction is not proof of understanding. Explain the sign, the input multiplier and what was held fixed.
calculus/debug.alt: Forward operations produce a sigmoid prediction and log-loss; backward sensitivities return through the score to weight and bias.

calculus/integrals.title: Accumulation is the other half of change
calculus/integrals.story: If speed is v(t)=10t metres per second, how far do you travel from 0 to 3 seconds? Thin time slices turn speed into small distances. Adding them approaches the area under the curve.
calculus/integrals.predict: Why do left-end rectangles underestimate this increasing speed while right-end rectangles overestimate it?
calculus/integrals.relationship: The definite integral ∫₀³ 10t dt = 45 measures accumulated distance. Differentiating the accumulated quantity recovers its rate; recovering position also needs an initial position.
calculus/integrals.ml: A probability density is not a probability at one point: area over an interval gives probability. Integration also expresses expectations of continuous quantities.
calculus/integrals.caution: This is an introductory, unscored reading extension. It adds no integral solver or completion requirement. Negative velocity would contribute signed displacement.
calculus/integrals.alt: Rectangles under a rising speed curve approach the triangular area 45; differentiating 5t² recovers speed 10t.

probability/understanding.title: Count the possibilities before trusting a hunch
probability/understanding.story: Two fair dice have 36 equally likely ordered outcomes. A total of 7 can occur in six different ways, while a total of 2 has only one. The sum is not uniformly distributed even though each die is fair.
probability/understanding.predict: Are totals 2 and 7 equally likely simply because both are possible?
probability/understanding.relationship: Probability compares an event with a specified sample space. “Equally likely” needs a reason, such as fair independent dice, rather than being an automatic property of possibilities.
probability/understanding.ml: Probability provides a language for uncertainty. A model score needs interpretation and validation before you call it a reliable probability.
probability/understanding.caution: Long-run frequencies stabilize under suitable sampling conditions. More samples do not automatically remove selection bias or make a model calibrated.
probability/understanding.alt: A six-by-six ordered dice grid highlights the six combinations summing to 7.

probability/multiple-events.title: AND and OR answer different questions
probability/multiple-events.story: Suppose passing exam A has probability 0.8 and passing B has probability 0.7. If the outcomes are independent, both passes have probability 0.56, while at least one pass has probability 0.94.
probability/multiple-events.predict: Why would adding 0.8 and 0.7 double-count some students?
probability/multiple-events.relationship: P(A or B) = P(A)+P(B)−P(A and B). Multiplying marginal probabilities for an intersection additionally requires independence.
probability/multiple-events.ml: Combining signals often requires dependence assumptions. Naive Bayes assumes features are conditionally independent given the class, not independent in the population overall.
probability/multiple-events.caution: A shared disruption could affect both exams, breaking independence. The current event playground uses message counts rather than these exam probabilities.
probability/multiple-events.alt: The overlap represents both passes, while the union includes either pass and counts the overlap once.

probability/conditional.title: Change the denominator when evidence arrives
probability/conditional.story: Among 1,000 emails, 200 are spam and 800 genuine. “Free” appears in 60% of spam and 5% of genuine messages. Once you see “free,” the relevant population becomes the 160 messages containing it.
probability/conditional.predict: Should the denominator still be all 1,000 messages after you know the message contains “free”?
probability/conditional.relationship: P(spam | free) = 120/160 = 0.75. Conditioning restricts the set of cases; it does not reverse the direction of the original 60% statement.
probability/conditional.ml: Evaluate a diagnostic signal within the population to which it is applied. A signal’s false positives can dominate when the target condition is rare.
probability/conditional.caution: P(free | spam) and P(spam | free) are different. This book example is separate from the playground’s message counts.
probability/conditional.alt: Of 160 messages containing “free,” 120 are spam and 40 are genuine; the conditional spam probability is 75%.

probability/bayes.title: Combine a prior with a signal’s strength
probability/bayes.story: Among 1,000 emails, 200 are spam. “Free” appears in 60% of spam and 5% of the 800 genuine emails: 120 + 40 = 160 messages. Start with the 20% spam prior, multiply by the 60% likelihood of “free” in spam, then divide by the overall 16% frequency of “free.”
probability/bayes.predict: If spam became much rarer but the signal rates stayed fixed, would seeing “free” still imply a 75% spam probability?
probability/bayes.relationship: Bayes’ rule updates a prior by accounting for how likely the evidence is under each possibility. A strong-looking signal is incomplete without its base rate.
probability/bayes.ml: Spam classification, medical screening and model comparison all need careful distinctions between a likelihood and an updated probability.
probability/bayes.caution: The existing diagnostic playground defaults to a 10% false-positive rate; the book’s medical example uses 9%. Those produce different posterior probabilities.
probability/bayes.alt: A prior population splits into spam and genuine messages before the word signal narrows the population.

probability/distributions.title: A distribution describes more than its average
probability/distributions.story: A fair die has mean 3.5 even though it can never show 3.5. A distribution assigns probabilities to possible values; its mean summarizes the balance point and its variance summarizes spread.
probability/distributions.predict: Can two distributions share a mean while placing their probability in very different places?
headers: Ten independent fair coins, heads count
probability/distributions.relationship: A random variable maps outcomes to numerical values. Discrete distributions assign point probabilities; continuous densities assign probability through area over intervals.
probability/distributions.ml: Noise, labels and predictions require distributional assumptions. A normal model can be useful without claiming that every real dataset is bell-shaped.
probability/distributions.caution: The central limit theorem concerns suitably scaled averages under conditions such as independence and finite variance. It does not make the original observations normal.
probability/distributions.alt: Die faces have equal probabilities but binomial coin-count probabilities concentrate near five heads.

probability/ml.title: Turn probability into a learning signal
probability/ml.story: Seven heads and three tails support a coin-bias estimate of 0.7 under an independent Bernoulli model. Instead of multiplying ten tiny factors, add their logarithms.
probability/ml.predict: Which model should assign more probability to this data: p=0.5 or p=0.7? Does a 0.8 prediction guarantee the next event?
probability/ml.relationship: Maximizing likelihood means selecting settings that assign high probability to the observed data under a specified model. Negative log-likelihood converts that objective into a loss to minimize.
probability/ml.ml: Softmax converts scores into positive values summing to one. Calibration asks whether groups of similarly scored predictions match observed frequencies.
probability/ml.caution: Normalization alone does not establish calibration. Not all ML algorithms are probabilistic, and not all training objectives are maximum likelihood.
probability/ml.alt: For seven heads and three tails, the likelihood and log-likelihood both peak at p=0.7.

statistics/data.title: Choose a picture that answers your question
statistics/data.story: Nine salaries, in thousands of rupees, are 25, 28, 30, 32, 35, 38, 40, 45 and 400. A single list conceals how far the founder’s salary sits from the rest. A suitable chart makes that difference visible.
statistics/data.predict: Would a bar chart of categories answer the same question as a histogram of salary values?
statistics/data.relationship: Data type and question determine the representation. Label units and scales so the reader can distinguish an observed measurement from a calculated summary.
statistics/data.ml: Before training a model, inspect missing values, unusual observations, distributions and relationships. A plot can expose a problem that a single metric conceals.
statistics/data.caution: An outlier is a reason to investigate, not automatic permission to delete an inconvenient observation.
statistics/data.alt: Four examples distinguish histograms, scatter plots, box plots and categorical bar charts.

statistics/center.title: A typical value depends on the question
statistics/center.story: The founder’s salary raises the nine-person mean to about ₹74,778, while the middle salary is ₹35,000. Both calculations are correct; they summarize different aspects of the same group.
statistics/center.predict: Which summary would better describe the salary a middle-ranked employee receives?
statistics/center.relationship: The mean balances every numerical value. The median identifies the middle of the ordered data and is less sensitive to extreme magnitudes. Neither replaces the distribution.
statistics/center.ml: Squared-error models target a conditional mean; absolute-error objectives target a conditional median under standard conditions. The loss helps determine what “best prediction” means.
statistics/center.caution: Do not remove the founder merely to obtain a nicer average. Define the population and report the choice.
statistics/center.alt: Eight salaries cluster near 25–45 thousand, while one lies at 400 thousand; mean and median fall in different places.

statistics/spread.title: The average cannot tell you the risk
statistics/spread.story: Two groups can share a mean while one clusters tightly and the other varies widely. Squaring deviations makes negative and positive differences contribute positively to spread.
statistics/spread.predict: What information disappears if you report only a mean and omit the spread?
statistics/spread.relationship: Population variance divides by N for the full specified population. A conventional sample-variance estimator divides by n−1 when estimating a population variance from a sample.
statistics/spread.ml: Feature scaling and error analysis depend on spread. A few large residuals can dominate squared error even if most predictions are close.
statistics/spread.caution: The book’s salary SD near 122 thousand uses the sample convention; the playground’s default variance convention is labelled separately. Compare like with like.
statistics/spread.alt: The isolated founder salary illustrates how an extreme value affects both average and spread.

statistics/distributions.title: Separate individual variation from average variation
statistics/distributions.story: Individual marks can vary substantially, while repeated averages of random samples vary less. With population SD 12 and n=36 independent observations, the standard error of the sample mean is 2.
statistics/distributions.predict: To halve the standard error, do you need twice as many observations or four times as many?
statistics/distributions.relationship: Standard deviation describes individual spread. Standard error describes how an estimator varies across repeated samples. Under suitable conditions, averages can have an approximately normal sampling distribution.
statistics/distributions.ml: Uncertainty about an estimated model metric differs from the variation among individual examples. Confidence intervals describe a procedure’s uncertainty, not a guarantee for each case.
statistics/distributions.caution: A normal approximation requires justification. A 95% confidence interval is not an interval containing 95% of individual observations.
statistics/distributions.alt: Individual student marks have a broad distribution; averages of repeated samples form a much narrower distribution.

statistics/relationships.title: A pattern can predict without explaining a cause
statistics/relationships.story: Study hours and marks may rise together, but the fitted relationship alone does not show that adding an hour will cause a particular increase for every student. Background factors may influence both.
statistics/relationships.predict: Could ice-cream sales and drownings move together because both respond to hot weather?
rows: Can one help predict the other?
Would an intervention change the outcome?
statistics/relationships.relationship: Correlation summarizes linear association. Regression describes a fitted conditional relationship. Neither automatically identifies an intervention’s effect.
statistics/relationships.ml: A predictive feature can be useful without being a safe lever to change. Compare out-of-sample performance and examine confounding and leakage.
statistics/relationships.caution: The book’s fitted marks line and reported correlation are illustrative; its raw dataset is not supplied for independent reproduction. The playground has its own explicit dataset and causal scenarios.
statistics/relationships.alt: Hot weather influences both ice-cream sales and swimming-related drowning exposure, creating a confounded association.

statistics/sampling.title: More data reduces variation, not every bias
statistics/sampling.story: Surveying only students in the library at midnight can give a precise answer about an unrepresentative group. Random variation and systematic selection bias are different problems.
statistics/sampling.predict: Would collecting ten times as many responses from the same biased location solve the sampling problem?
rows: 95% probability for a fixed parameter after sampling
Data are unusual under a specified null model
Probability the null hypothesis is true
statistics/sampling.relationship: For mean 62, known population SD 12 and n=36, an approximate normal interval is 62 ± 1.96×2 = [58.08, 65.92]. If population SD is unknown, an appropriate t procedure may be needed.
statistics/sampling.ml: A/B tests need a valid design, independent experimental units and prespecified analysis. Statistical significance and practical usefulness answer different questions.
statistics/sampling.caution: For 100/1000 versus 120/1000 independent conversions, a pooled two-sided normal test gives z≈1.429 and p≈0.153. This is not the probability the observed improvement is a fluke.
statistics/sampling.alt: Repeatedly constructed confidence intervals vary; most cover the fixed population mean, while some miss it.

statistics/ml.title: Judge predictions with the errors that matter
statistics/ml.story: A spam classifier faces 1,000 messages: 80 true positives, 20 missed spam, 30 false alarms and 870 true negatives. Its 95% accuracy hides two very different kinds of error.
statistics/ml.predict: If blocking a genuine message is costly, is accuracy alone enough to choose the model?
statistics/ml.relationship: Precision asks how many flagged cases were correct; recall asks how many actual positives were found. Threshold choice changes the trade-off.
statistics/ml.ml: Fit on training data, select settings on validation data, and reserve a final test set for the final evaluation. Cross-validation supports development without making the final test a tuning tool.
statistics/ml.caution: The book’s polynomial comparison uses “test” while discussing model selection. Here that development role is validation. A train–evaluation gap can reflect overfitting, distribution shift or other split problems.
statistics/ml.alt: A confusion matrix separates 80 correct spam flags, 20 misses, 30 false alarms and 870 correct genuine predictions.

optimization/objectives.title: Best is meaningless until you name the objective
optimization/objectives.story: A bakery earns ₹60 per cake and ₹40 per tart. Flour allows 2x+y≤16 and oven time allows x+y≤10. The goal is not simply to make more items, but to maximize profit within both limits.
optimization/objectives.predict: Could a profitable combination still be impossible because it exceeds a resource limit?
optimization/objectives.relationship: An objective ranks choices; constraints define which choices are allowed. In this linear example, comparing feasible corners identifies the maximum of ₹520 at (6,4).
optimization/objectives.ml: Training minimizes an explicit loss, often with penalties or constraints. Business value and training loss are related design choices, not interchangeable quantities.
optimization/objectives.caution: For real products, counts must be whole numbers. This example’s best corner already has integer coordinates. General constrained problems need not be solved by this simple corner comparison.
optimization/objectives.alt: Flour and oven constraints bound a feasible region; the highest-profit shown corner is six cakes and four tarts.

optimization/updates.title: Use the slope to choose a small next move
optimization/updates.story: A gradient tells you how an objective changes locally. Subtracting a scaled gradient proposes a move toward lower loss, but a step that is too large can jump across a valley and increase the loss.
optimization/updates.predict: On L(w)=(w−3)², starting at w=1, what does a learning rate of 0.1 do?
optimization/updates.relationship: The update w_new = w_old − η∇L uses the gradient at the old point. The learning rate η sets the scale of the move. Local improvement is not a proof of global convergence.
optimization/updates.ml: Batch methods use a full dataset gradient; stochastic and mini-batch methods estimate it from selected examples. Momentum carries a moving velocity; Adam tracks gradient moments.
optimization/updates.caution: The current playground implements its labelled update rule, not momentum or Adam. Their book descriptions are an introductory comparison, not new optimizer functionality.
optimization/updates.alt: Gradient descent zigzags in a narrow valley; a momentum illustration follows a smoother trajectory under the book’s chosen settings.

optimization/geometry.title: The landscape explains why some paths are difficult
optimization/geometry.story: A bowl, a saddle and a landscape with several valleys can all have flat points. Their shapes determine what a gradient can tell you and how much a local solution promises.
optimization/geometry.predict: Does zero gradient guarantee a minimum? Does convexity always mean exactly one minimum?
rows: Every local minimum is global, if a minimum exists
Some directions rise while others fall
Different local minima may have different values
optimization/geometry.relationship: Curvature describes how slope changes. Narrow valleys have very different sensitivities across directions; a step suitable for a shallow direction may overshoot in a steep one.
optimization/geometry.ml: Feature scaling and parameterization affect training geometry. Convexity is useful, but convergence still requires appropriate assumptions and step choices.
optimization/geometry.caution: The book overstates uniqueness for convex functions. A constant function is convex and has many minimizers; even a convex objective need not attain a minimum.
optimization/geometry.alt: A saddle rises in one coordinate direction and falls in the other, despite a zero gradient at its centre.

optimization/stability.title: A faster-looking step can be the wrong step
optimization/stability.story: Repeated updates can converge, oscillate or diverge. Compare the objective values along the path rather than judging a method by a single large movement.
optimization/stability.predict: If successive losses grow, would simply running more iterations repair the update rule?
rows: Can fail with zero or unsuitable curvature
optimization/stability.relationship: For a quadratic, a suitable Newton step can reach its stationary point exactly. Root finding instead uses x_new=x−f(x)/f′(x); these are related but different tasks.
optimization/stability.ml: Schedules, momentum and curvature-aware methods change how updates behave. Choose and validate them for the objective rather than treating one method as universally best.
optimization/stability.caution: Newton and adaptive optimizers are reading extensions here. The existing finite trace establishes what happened for its stated settings, not a universal convergence guarantee.
optimization/stability.alt: Newton root-finding uses the tangent to x²−2 at x=2 to propose x=1.5, then approaches √2.

optimization/regularization.title: Change what counts as a good fit
optimization/regularization.story: A data loss prefers w=3. Adding λw² penalizes large weights, so the best total objective may move away from the best data-only fit. Regularization is a deliberate trade-off.
optimization/regularization.predict: With λ=1, should the new optimum remain 3, become zero, or sit between them?
optimization/regularization.relationship: For (w−3)²+λw², set 2(w−3)+2λw=0. The resulting optimum balances fit and penalty rather than minimizing either term separately.
optimization/regularization.ml: L2 penalties shrink weights; L1 penalties can encourage exact zeros. Use validation to assess whether a penalty improves generalization.
optimization/regularization.caution: Scaling affects penalties. L1 does not guarantee selection of the truly relevant features, and adaptive weight decay is not generally identical to adding an L2 loss term.
optimization/regularization.alt: As the L2 penalty grows, the optimal weight for this scalar problem shrinks from 3 toward zero.

optimization/responsible.title: Select a model without peeking at its final exam
optimization/responsible.story: A model can keep improving on training data while validation loss rises. Early stopping chooses a development checkpoint; the final test set must stay out of that decision.
optimization/responsible.predict: If you repeatedly select settings using final-test results, is that set still an independent final check?
rows: Input values, arithmetic and step size
Potential overfitting, split quality or distribution shift
Cannot fit a tiny clean batch
optimization/responsible.relationship: Hyperparameter search and early stopping are model-selection procedures. Compare on validation evidence, preserve the chosen checkpoint, then use the held-out test for final evaluation.
optimization/responsible.ml: A useful training run is reproducible: record data split, preprocessing, settings and random seeds where relevant. Metric improvements need a meaningful evaluation context.
optimization/responsible.caution: The plotted best epoch is an illustrative book run, not a universal stopping point or a result from this playground. Diagnose symptoms rather than blindly increasing or decreasing the learning rate.
optimization/responsible.alt: Training loss keeps falling while validation loss bottoms out near epoch 18 and rises afterward; early stopping restores the development checkpoint.

algebra/transformations.title: Order changes the answer
algebra/transformations.story: A ₹1,000 item gets a ₹100 discount and an 18% tax. Applying the discount first gives a different total from taxing first. A chain of simple rules is a new rule—and its order matters.
algebra/transformations.predict: Would the same two operations necessarily give the same result in either order?
algebra/transformations.relationship: g(f(x)) means apply f first, then g. Transformations change a graph systematically: f(x)+k moves it vertically; f(x−h) moves it right by h.
algebra/transformations.ml: A preprocessing step followed by a model is a composition. Neural networks compose matrix operations and nonlinear activations; those nonlinearities prevent the whole network collapsing to one matrix product.
algebra/transformations.caution: Changing preprocessing order can change predictions. A quadratic shifted right by 3 uses (x−3)², not (x+3)².
algebra/transformations.alt: Discount then tax produces ₹1,062, while tax then discount produces ₹1,080.
